I would not describe one future. I would describe the trade-off in each of them.

I ask every founder the same question in the first meeting, and I am not looking for a forecast. Nobody in this business believes a five-year forecast, including the person presenting it. What I am listening for is whether this is a person who has ever seriously considered a company other than the one he already decided to build. When the answer comes back as bigger, more clients, more countries, I stop listening, because that is not a future. That is the same company with larger numbers on it, and it tells me the founder has never once sat down and imagined losing something. What I want is two versions, and the trade-off between them. Tell me the one where you keep control and grow slowly, tell me the one where you take money and move fast, tell me what you would give up in each, and then tell me which one you would take and why. A founder who can do that in four minutes is a founder I can work with for eight years.

Founders count the wrong number. They watch the percentage, because the percentage is on the page in front of them, and they stop counting the thing that actually changes, which is how many decisions they can still make alone. I raised at the end of my fourth year. I still owned a majority afterwards, comfortably, and by the middle of the second year after that round I was explaining a single hiring decision to three people before I made it. Nobody blocked me. Nobody had to. The explaining is the cost, and the explaining does not show up anywhere in the ownership table. If I were doing it again, I would do exactly one thing differently. I would write down, before the money arrived, which decisions I wanted to keep for myself. Not the big ones, because everybody protects the big ones. The ordinary ones. Because after the round, the ordinary decisions are the ones that quietly stop being yours, and by the time you notice, the habit is already built.

Let me give you two versions, not one. In the first, we reinvest everything and headcount grows slowly. In the second, we raise, and the dilution would take me close to forty percent. So the trade-off is the same in both: speed or control. If I had to choose today, I would take the second one. And now I would like to hear which one you would take.
